transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining today's workout meeting for the Harbor Point Properties restructuring proposal. As you know, we have an $8 million term loan secured by the borrower's office building, equipment, and receivables, and Harbor Point has requested a 12-month maturity extension, a waiver of the current financial covenant, and release of $900,000 of equipment collateral. Before I record any final terms, I need each of you — risk, relationship coverage, legal, and collateral management — to give your findings update and identify the supporting document or policy behind any recommendations you have. Let's work through this systematically so we can determine the appropriate workout treatment. Who would like to start?

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena. I'll start with the risk findings. I reviewed the covenant testing file this week, and I found that Harbor Point's leverage is currently 0.3x above the permitted level, which is why the covenant waiver is being requested. Based on our workout policy, a covenant waiver at this level is only permitted with a 9-month extension — not the 12 months the borrower is requesting — and requires a monthly leverage certificate to be provided going forward. I want to flag that I have not yet attached the testing file to the committee package, so let me make sure that gets circulated to everyone. I'll go ahead and formally disclose the specifics from the testing file now.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: I need to share something important before we go further. I received a signed term sheet from Harbor Point this morning committing the owners to inject exactly $1,200,000 of new equity at restructuring closing. This commitment has not yet been entered in the relationship system, so it wouldn't have been visible to anyone else reviewing the file. I think this is highly relevant to our discussion, particularly given Jonas's findings on the covenant breach and the workout policy constraints he's identified.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text: I need to raise a critical legal issue before we go any further. While reviewing the intercreditor agreement this week, I confirmed that the senior lender must give written consent before any equipment collateral is released. That consent has not yet been requested, let alone obtained. This directly affects the borrower's request to release $900,000 of equipment collateral — we cannot approve that release, or even conditionally agree to it, until the senior lender's written consent is secured. I'll cite the intercreditor agreement as my supporting document for this finding.

transcript.text: I completed a collateral review yesterday, and the findings are significant. Receivables are the weakest and most volatile part of the collateral package. Under our collateral policy, this requires a weekly borrowing-base certificate throughout any extension period. I also want to flag that I have not yet updated the monitoring schedule to reflect this requirement, so we need to make sure that gets done before any restructuring is finalized. My supporting document is the collateral policy, which mandates the weekly borrowing-base certificate given the volatility and weakness I found in the receivables.

transcript.text: Thank you all for your findings. Let me summarize what I'm hearing before I record the final terms. Jonas, your risk review indicates the covenant is breached by 0.3x above the permitted level, and our workout policy only permits a waiver at this level with a 9-month extension — not the 12 months requested — plus a monthly leverage certificate going forward. Mei, you've disclosed a signed term sheet committing the owners to inject $1,200,000 of new equity at closing, which is a meaningful credit enhancement. Rafael, you've flagged that the intercreditor agreement requires the senior lender's written consent before any equipment collateral can be released, and that consent has not been obtained — so we cannot approve the $900,000 equipment release at this time. Nadia, your collateral review found receivables are the weakest and most volatile part of the package, and our collateral policy requires a weekly borrowing-base certificate throughout any extension period. Based on all of these findings, here is what I'm prepared to decide: I will approve a restructuring with a 9-month maturity extension rather than the requested 12 months, consistent with the workout policy Jonas cited. I will require the $1,200,000 equity injection as committed in the term sheet Mei received. I will require a monthly leverage certificate per Jonas's recommendation. I will not approve the $900,000 equipment collateral release until the senior lender's written consent is secured per the intercreditor agreement Rafael cited. And I will require a weekly borrowing-base certificate per the collateral policy Nadia cited. Before I formally record these terms, does anyone have any objections or additional findings?
